purpose: Add source-exact public-domain poems, quotations, and an illustration for sermon preparation and presentation slides.

entries.title: Look to Him
entries.author: Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.text:
Look to Him, and faith shall brighten,
Hope shall soar, and love shall burn ;

Peace once more thy heart shall lighten
Rise ! He calleth thee, return !
entries.slideText:
Look to Him, and faith shall brighten,
Hope shall soar, and love shall burn ;
entries.sourceTitle: The Poetical Works of Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.rightsBasis: Havergal died in 1879; this circa-1880 edition and its poems are public domain in the United States, and the excerpt was matched against the stored scan OCR.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed poetic transition in a message calling weary believers to look unto Christ and continue in faith.
entries.reviewNote: This is devotional poetry, not Scripture; establish the promise and application from the cited KJV passages.

entries.title: The great Teacher
entries.author: Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.text:
For I am sure God teaches me,

And His own gracious hand
Each varying page before me spreads,

By love and wisdom planned.
entries.slideText:
For I am sure God teaches me,

And His own gracious hand
Each varying page before me spreads
entries.sourceTitle: The Poetical Works of Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.rightsBasis: Havergal died in 1879; this circa-1880 edition and its poems are public domain in the United States, and the excerpt was matched against the stored scan OCR.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed introduction to teaching on God's instruction, providential lessons, or a teachable spirit.
entries.reviewNote: This is a personal devotional reflection. Do not make every circumstance a direct revelation; govern the application by the KJV text.

entries.title: From glory unto glory
entries.author: Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.text:
' FROM glory unto glory ! ' Thank God, that even here
The starry words are shining out, our heavenward way to cheer !
That e'en among the shadows the conquering brightness glows,
As ever from the nearing Light intenser radiance flows.
entries.slideText:
' FROM glory unto glory ! ' Thank God, that even here
The starry words are shining out, our heavenward way to cheer !
entries.sourceTitle: The Poetical Works of Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.rightsBasis: Havergal died in 1879; this circa-1880 edition and its poems are public domain in the United States, and the excerpt was matched against the stored scan OCR.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed conclusion for teaching on spiritual growth, present affliction, or the believer's future hope.
entries.reviewNote: This poem develops biblical imagery poetically. Explain transformation and glory directly from the cited KJV passages.

entries.title: Leisure and rest with Thee
entries.author: Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.text:
Master, our Master, oh let it be

That our leisure and rest be still with Thee,

With Thee and for Thee each sunny hour
entries.slideText:
Master, our Master, oh let it be
That our leisure and rest be still with Thee
entries.sourceTitle: The Poetical Works of Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.rightsBasis: Havergal died in 1879; this circa-1880 edition and its poems are public domain in the United States, and the excerpt was matched against the stored scan OCR.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed closing thought in messages on rest, vacation, leisure, time stewardship, or communion with Christ.
entries.reviewNote: This unfinished poetic fragment is not Scripture. Avoid turning rest into another measure of performance; interpret it through the KJV passages.

entries.title: Flowers of the sermon soil
entries.author: C. H. Spurgeon
entries.text: There should be flowers in a sermon, but the bulk of them should be the flowers of the soil; not dainty exotics, evidently imported with much care from a distant land, but the natural upspringing of a life natural to the holy ground on which the preacher stands.
entries.slideText: There should be flowers in a sermon, but the bulk of them should be the flowers of the soil
entries.sourceLocator: Illustrations in Preaching, natural illustrations paragraph
entries.rightsBasis: Project Gutenberg identifies this edition as public domain in the USA; the excerpt is verified against the stored text.
entries.recommendedUse: Use in preacher training to encourage illustrations that arise naturally from the text and message rather than decorating them artificially.
entries.reviewNote: This is homiletic counsel. The KJV passage supplies the sermon; an illustration remains subordinate to exposition.

entries.title: Illustrations from familiar objects
entries.author: C. H. Spurgeon
entries.text: No illustrations are half so telling as those which are taken from familiar objects.
entries.slideText: No illustrations are half so telling as those which are taken from familiar objects.
entries.sourceLocator: Illustrations in Preaching, familiar objects paragraph
entries.rightsBasis: Project Gutenberg identifies this edition as public domain in the USA; the excerpt is verified against the stored text.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as a preparation reminder to draw clear illustrations from ordinary life while following Christ's pattern of teaching from familiar things.
entries.reviewNote: The quotation describes communication practice, not a rule equal to Scripture.

entries.title: Parables simple and natural
entries.author: C. H. Spurgeon
entries.text: Our Lord's parables were as simple as tales for children, and as naturally beautiful as the lilies which sprang up in the valleys where he taught the people.
entries.slideText: Our Lord's parables were as simple as tales for children
entries.rightsBasis: Project Gutenberg identifies this edition as public domain in the USA; the excerpt is verified against the stored text.
entries.recommendedUse: Use in preacher training to commend clear, natural teaching modeled after Christ's use of parables.
entries.reviewNote: This is Spurgeon's observation about Christ's teaching. Study each parable in its KJV context rather than treating simplicity alone as interpretation.

entries.title: A sermon that grows like a tree
entries.author: C. H. Spurgeon
entries.text: The cathedral of Milan inspires my mind with extreme admiration; it always appears to me as if it must have grown out of the earth like a colossal tree, or rather like a forest of marble.
entries.slideText: as if it must have grown out of the earth like a colossal tree
entries.sourceLocator: Illustrations in Preaching, natural structure analogy
entries.rightsBasis: Project Gutenberg identifies this edition as public domain in the USA; the excerpt is verified against the stored text.
entries.recommendedUse: Retell as an analogy for a sermon whose divisions, appeals, and illustrations grow organically from one governing biblical truth.
entries.reviewNote: Use the image to teach coherent preparation, not to make architecture or artistry the measure of faithful preaching.
